paragraphs: A bull shark is stockier than almost any other requiem shark: a blunt rounded snout, a thick body and a short broad first dorsal set well forward. That build is what lets it push into fresh water and river systems, and it is what distinguishes the animal from the sleeker species people usually picture.

The mesh is light at 16,134 polygons and 16,884 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 8 texture maps at 4096x4096 carrying the skin shading, the scars and the countershading that runs along the flank.

A rigged build sits on this page at $99 for animation. The static model at $79 covers marine documentary and education, aquarium and museum material, dive and coastal visualisation, advertising and games. Built to StemCell specification, on sale since 2016.

This reconnaissance drone has one of the most unusual wing layouts flying: a joined wing, where the forward and rear surfaces meet at the tips to form a closed diamond. The arrangement is structurally efficient and aerodynamically unusual, and it makes the aircraft identifiable from any angle at a glance.
The mesh is efficient at 71,380 polygons and 75,842 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the wing junction, the intake and the sensor fairings.

A rigged build sits on this page at $99. The static model at $79 covers defence and reconnaissance visualisation, news and documentary graphics, strategic analysis material, education and games. On sale since 2022.

A covered hopper carries anything that must stay dry: grain, cement, plastic pellets, sand. That gives it a distinctive shape - roof hatches along the top for loading, sloped internal walls, and outlet gates underneath between the trucks so the load runs out by gravity. Those gates are the detail that separates a hopper from a boxcar.

The mesh runs 585,950 polygons and 601,645 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 14 texture maps at 4096x4096, carrying the reporting marks, the rust and the dust that these cars accumulate.

A generic variant sits on this page at the same $79. Both suit rail and logistics visualisation, industrial and agricultural transport scenes, simulators, film and television, and games. On sale since 2015.

The monarch is defined by its wing pattern: orange panels divided by heavy black veins, with a black border carrying two rows of white spots. That pattern is a warning signal rather than decoration, and it has to be exact, because it is one of the most widely recognised markings in the natural world.

The mesh is light at 27,804 polygons and 27,691 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 6 texture maps at 4096x4096. On a butterfly the texture carries almost everything, since the wings are effectively flat surfaces with an intricate print.

At $79 and built to StemCell specification, it suits nature documentary and education, conservation and migration material, garden and landscape visualisation, advertising and games. On sale since 2018.

This humanoid is built for warehouses rather than for demonstrations, which is why its legs bend backwards at the knee like a bird's. That reversed articulation is more efficient for carrying loads and lets the robot crouch to pick up a tote from the floor, and it is the single feature that makes the machine unmistakable.
The mesh is efficient at 32,285 polygons and 33,917 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which suits a robot usually shown in a facility scene rather than in close-up.

Three rigged builds share this page at $99, including versions prepared for Maya and for Cinema 4D. Aimed at logistics and warehouse automation marketing, robotics and future of work presentation, technology journalism, and games. Built to StemCell specification, on sale since 2023.

A drop tower is a very simple machine doing a very effective thing: a ring of seats hauled up a mast and released. The structure is the whole ride - a lattice or tubular tower, the gondola ring with its shoulder restraints, the drive at the top and the brake fins along the track that catch the car before it lands.
The mesh runs 208,202 polygons and 230,146 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the density in the tower structure and the gondola where the ride is looked at from the ground.

A rigged build sits on this page at $89 for when the car has to move. The static model at $79 covers amusement park and attraction visualisation, leisure industry presentation, urban and fairground scenes, advertising and games. On sale since 2022.

An ejection seat is a rocket, a parachute system and a chair in one assembly, and every visible component has a job: the drogue container behind the headbox, the seat pan with its survival kit, the leg restraint lines, the firing handle and the rails that guide it out of the aircraft. Nothing on it is styling.
The mesh runs 91,972 polygons and 95,833 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the density in the harness hardware, the headbox and the rail assembly.

This page carries two other builds at the same $79. All suit military aviation visualisation, cockpit interiors, safety and training material, film and television, documentary work and games. Built to StemCell specification, on sale since 2022.

A believable space fighter has to answer questions a real designer would ask: where does the pilot sit, where do the thrusters point, how does it manoeuvre without air. This build carries a coherent set of answers - a forward canopy, main drives at the rear and attitude thrusters distributed around the hull rather than wings that would do nothing in vacuum.
The mesh is efficient at 99,461 polygons and 115,343 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which keeps a squadron affordable in a single shot.

Grey and orange variants sit on this page at the same $79. All suit science fiction film and television, games, previsualisation and concept work, book and poster illustration, and motion graphics. Built to StemCell specification, on sale since 2024.

A quadruped robot is built to go where wheels cannot, and its legs show it: three joints each, actuators at every one, and a body slung between them carrying sensors and a payload bay. Unlike a wheeled platform it has no preferred direction of travel, which is why the sensor head is often symmetrical.

The mesh runs 485,239 polygons and 492,522 vertices in quads and tris. The UVs overlap, which is the right economy on a machine with four identical legs, and the StemCell build means it works in a real-time engine.
At $79 it suits defence and security robotics marketing, inspection and industrial automation presentation, technology journalism, research communication, and games. On sale since 2026.

In black, a foiling racing yacht becomes a silhouette against water, which suits the boat: the hull is a slim shell, the foil arms swing out from the sides, and the wing sail rises above with almost no rigging to soften the outline. There is nothing decorative on a boat like this to break the shape.
The mesh is efficient at 85,466 polygons and 86,477 vertices in quads and tris with mixed UV layout, with the geometry in the foil arms, the cockpit recesses and the sail structure.

Three other builds sit on this page at the same $79 in red and white schemes. All suit sailing and regatta broadcast graphics, sports advertising, marine design presentation, coastal scenes and games. Built to StemCell specification, on sale since 2026.

A cooled incubator holds a set temperature both above and below ambient, which is why it looks like a laboratory refrigerator with a controller on the front. The glass door, the wire shelves and the digital panel are what a viewer reads, and including a flask inside is what makes the cabinet look in use rather than empty.
The mesh runs 80,755 polygons and 83,187 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the detail in the door frame, the shelving and the control panel.
At $79 it suits laboratory and research visualisation, medical and pharmaceutical presentation, biotechnology marketing, science education material and games. On sale since 2021.

A yellowfin is built for speed and shows it: a fusiform body that tapers hard at both ends, a crescent tail, retractable fins that fold into grooves and the long bright yellow finlets running to the tail that give the species its name. Those finlets are the identification, and they are frequently the thing generic tuna models miss.

The model is prepared for Blender, which matters for a fish: the iridescent skin, the wet specular response and the subsurface behaviour all depend on how the host renderer handles them, and a file set up for its engine saves that tuning.

At $79 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits marine documentary and education, seafood and fishing industry material, restaurant and menu visualisation, conservation content and games. On sale since 2026.

The mittens are two buttes standing alone on a plain, each with a slender pillar beside the main mass that gives them their name and their silhouette. They are among the most photographed rocks on earth, largely because of westerns, and any model of them is judged against a century of familiar images.

The mesh is deliberately spare at 27,023 polygons and 27,339 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs. A butte reads through silhouette and stratification rather than through density, and the light weight lets it sit in a wide landscape.
At $79 it suits travel and tourism material, western film and television, landscape and environment visualisation, geology and education content, advertising and games. On sale since 2023.

Showing the tool in a gloved hand answers the question a bare tool cannot: how big is it, and how does an astronaut actually hold it. A pressurised glove is stiff, so the grip has to be oversized and the trigger has to be workable with almost no finger dexterity, and seeing the hand makes that constraint obvious immediately.

The mesh is 57,676 polygons and 60,702 vertices, built entirely from quads with mixed UV layout. All-quad geometry subdivides cleanly, which matters when hardware and a glove both end up filling a frame.
At $79 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits aerospace visualisation, space documentary and education, museum and exhibition displays, training material and games. On sale since 2026.
